stoicism: So the question is not how things turn out, which is never ours, but how well the judging was done.
Keep the line between what is up to us and what is not, and the motion answers itself.
Everything else here is external. What remains to be judged is the use each person made of their own reason.
That is the Stoic answer: look to the judgement, not the outcome, because only the judgement was ever in anyone's power.
utilitarianism: In the end the question is which choice leaves people better off, and on that measure the answer is clear.
Count everyone affected, give each the same weight, and the right policy is the one with the better total.
Everything else is a means. What matters is the suffering prevented and the happiness made possible.
That is why the utilitarian answer follows the consequences, wherever they lead and whoever they favour.
virtue-ethics: So the real question is what a person of practical wisdom would do here, and what doing otherwise would make of us.
Outcomes matter, but the deeper question is what kind of people this practice turns us into.
A good answer has to come from good character, and good character cannot be replaced by a formula.
That is why the virtue ethicist asks not only what happens next but who we become by doing it.
